*[Bug 19119] New: `writeChar()` on Windows counts supplementary characters twice*
<https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=19119>

            Bug ID: 19119
           Summary: `writeChar()` on Windows counts supplementary
                    characters twice
           Product: R
           Version: R-devel (trunk)
          Hardware: Other
                OS: Other
            Status: NEW
          Severity: normal
          Priority: P5
         Component: Low-level
          Assignee: <mailto:R-core@R-project.org|R-core@R-project.org>
          Reporter: <mailto:kevinushey@gmail.com|kevinushey@gmail.com>

## Summary

`do_writechar()` counts the characters of each element with
`mbstowcs(NULL, s, 0)`.  Where `wchar_t` is 16-bit (Windows), `mbstowcs()`
returns the number of UTF-16 code units, so each supplementary ("non-BMP")
character such as `"\U0001F600"` counts as 2.  `nchars` therefore means
something different on Windows than on other platforms -- and something
different from what `readChar()` and `nchar()` mean by a "char" on Windows
itself.  `?writeChar` describes `nchars` as a number of characters, with no
platform qualification.

This surfaced as a Windows check failure of the regression test added with
the PR#19112 fix in r90334: the test writes 100 supplementary characters with
`nchars = 399L` and expects a 699-byte file; Windows writes 599 bytes.

## Reproducible example

Run on Windows, in a UTF-8 locale:

```
su <- strrep("\U0001F600", 100L)   # 100 characters, 400 bytes in UTF-8
nchar(su, "chars")
## [1] 100                <- R counts code points itself, also on Windows

tf <- tempfile(); f <- file(tf, "wb")
suppressWarnings(writeChar(su, f, nchars = 399L, eos = NULL))
close(f)
file.size(tf)
## Unix, macOS: 699       (400 bytes + 299 padding: 399 - 100 characters)
## Windows:     599       (400 bytes + 199 padding: 399 - 200 UTF-16 units)
```

This is part (c) of the PR#19112 regression test in `tests/reg-encodings.R`,
whose unconditional `stopifnot(all.equal(file.size(tf), 699))` currently
fails on Windows.

## Analysis

Both the buffer-sizing loop and the writing loop of `do_writechar()` count
characters the same way (`src/main/connections.c:5419-5420` and `:5506`):

```
            size_t nb = strlen(ss),
                nc = mbcslocale ? mbstowcs(NULL, ss, 0) : nb;
```

With a 16-bit `wchar_t`, converting a supplementary character yields a UTF-16
surrogate pair, so `mbstowcs(NULL, s, 0)` counts it twice.  The padding
arithmetic `nb += tt - nc` then under-pads by one byte per supplementary
character.

`readChar()` never goes through `wchar_t`: in a UTF-8 locale,
`readFixedString()` and `rawFixedString()` walk the input with `utf8clen()`,
one character at a time (`connections.c:5189-5212`, `:5245-5259`), and
`nchar(x, "chars")` likewise counts code points.  So on Windows,
`writeChar(x, con, nchars = n)` and `readChar(con, nchars = n)` disagree
about what a "char" is whenever `x` contains supplementary characters.

The truncation branch (`nchars` smaller than the character count,
`connections.c:5423-5433` and the matching loop in the writer) compares
`tt < nc` against the same inflated count before consuming characters with
`Mbrtowc()`; for non-BMP input this path was exercised by no test on any
platform.

## Candidate patch

Add `mbCharCount()` and `mbBytesForChars()` helpers used by both the
buffer-sizing loop and the writing loop: in a UTF-8 locale, count complete
UTF-8 characters directly via `utf8clen()` -- the same idiom `readChar()`
uses -- and in other MBCS locales keep the existing `mbstowcs()`/`Mbrtowc()`
code (those encodings have no supplementary-plane characters, so the counts
agree).

   mbstowcs() returns the number of UTF-16 code units, counting each
   supplementary ("non-BMP") character twice, so in a UTF-8 locale count

Properties:

- On platforms with 32-bit `wchar_t` (Unix, macOS), behavior is unchanged:
  for valid strings, the `utf8clen()` walk returns exactly what
  `mbstowcs()`/`Mbrtowc()` returned.
- Invalid multibyte strings take the previous `Mbrtowc()` path unchanged

- On Windows, `nchars` now counts supplementary characters once,
  consistently with `readChar()` and `nchar()`, and the unconditional
  `file.size(tf) == 699` expectation in `tests/reg-encodings.R` holds on
  Windows too.

The patch also adds a truncation test (`nchars` smaller than the number of
characters) with supplementary characters.  Its assertions deliberately use
`readBin()`/raw comparisons rather than `readChar()`: whether UCRT's
`mbrtowc()` (used in `readFixedString()`'s per-character validity check)
accepts 4-byte UTF-8 sequences with a 16-bit `wchar_t` is a separate open
question, and `readChar()` of non-BMP text on Windows deserves its own
test and investigation.

This changes what Windows writes for the (rare) case
`nchars != number of characters` with non-BMP input: previously-written
padded files effectively used UTF-16-unit counts.  Given that the
padding/truncation path for non-BMP characters was inconsistent between
`writeChar()` and `readChar()` and untested, treating the old Windows
behavior as a bug seems right, but that is R-core's call.  The alternative
is to keep the Windows behavior, special-case the r90334 regression test
(`if(onWindows) 599`, proposed as

), and document that on Windows
`nchars` counts UTF-16 code units.

On all platforms, including Windows:

su <- strrep("\U0001F600", 100L)

## (c) of the PR#19112 regression test: padding
tf <- tempfile(); f <- file(tf, "wb")
suppressWarnings(writeChar(su, f, nchars = 399L, eos = NULL))
close(f)
stopifnot(file.size(tf) == 699)

## truncation, previously untested for non-BMP input on any platform
r2 <- writeChar(su, raw(), nchars = 50L, eos = NULL)
tf2 <- tempfile(); f <- file(tf2, "wb")
writeChar(su, f, nchars = 50L, eos = NULL)
close(f)
stopifnot(exprs = {
    identical(r2, charToRaw(strrep("\U0001F600", 50L)))
    file.size(tf2) == 200
    identical(readBin(tf2, "raw", 300L), charToRaw(strrep("\U0001F600", 50L)))
})
```

and both Windows runners (x86_64 and aarch64).

*[Bug 19120] New: tools:::ccE() hard-codes 'cc', aborting "checking compiled code" on Windows*
<https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=19120>

            Bug ID: 19120
           Summary: tools:::ccE() hard-codes 'cc', aborting "checking
                    compiled code" on Windows
           Product: R
           Version: R-devel (trunk)
          Hardware: Other
                OS: Windows 64-bit
            Status: UNCONFIRMED
          Severity: normal
          Priority: P5
         Component: Models
          Assignee: <mailto:R-core@R-project.org|R-core@R-project.org>
          Reporter: <mailto:Ramirez-Lopez.L@buchi.com|Ramirez-Lopez.L@buchi.com>

On Windows, the "checking compiled code" step of R CMD check falls over for any
package with a src/ directory:

Like this:

```
* checking compiled code ... NOTE
Error in ccE(lines, flags = new_flags, include = include) : 
  'cc' is not on the path
Calls: <Anonymous> ... lapply -> FUN -> lapply -> FUN -> getFunsHdr -> ccE
Execution halted
```

The step never gets as far as looking at the package, so the NOTE says nothing
about the package itself... and the boilerplate that follows it ("See 'Writing
portable packages' ...") is a bit misleading, since nothing was actually
inspected. The practical upshot is that no C API-compliance checking is
happening on Windows at all at the moment, for any package with compiled code.
Maintainers also get a NOTE they can't do anything about, which takes some
explaining in cran-comments.

The cause is that tools:::ccE() wants a compiler literally called 'cc', both in
its guard and in the command it builds:

```
if (Sys.which("cc") == "") stop("'cc' is not on the path")
...
cmd <- sprintf("cc -E %s %s", include, tfile)
```

Rtools ships gcc.exe and g++.exe, and there's no cc anywhere on the path. 'cc'
is a normal enough name on Unix-alikes, but nothing provides it on Windows.

Easy to reproduce on Windows R-devel:

```
Sys.which("cc")
## ""
tools:::ccE("#include <Rinternals.h>")
## Error in tools:::ccE("#include <Rinternals.h>") : 
##   'cc' is not on the path
```

Or just run R CMD check on anything with a src/ directory.

Seen on:
- Local: R Under development (unstable) (2026-08-02 r90339 ucrt),
x86_64-w64-mingw32/x64
- CRAN Windows builder: R Under development (unstable) (2026-07-30 r90327
ucrt), Rtools gcc 14.3.0, Windows Server 2022

Martin Maechler mentioned he'd hit the same thing on win-builder (email,
2026-08-03).

One further thought, beyond the Windows breakage: even where 'cc' does exist it
isn't necessarily the compiler R was built with — it's usually a distro-managed
symlink. Since ccE() preprocesses R's own headers, a mismatch in predefined
macros, include paths or default C standard could give answers that don't match
how the package actually gets compiled. R CMD config CC would give the
configured compiler everywhere.

Martin Maechler (maechler@stat.math.ethz.ch) changed:

           What    |Removed                     |Added

--- Comment #4 from Martin Maechler (maechler@stat.math.ethz.ch) ---
(In reply to Suharto Anggono from comment #2)
>     x <- integer(0)
>     dim(x) <- c(1073741824L, 1073741824L, 0L)
> 
> as well as
> 
>     x <- array(integer(0), dim = c(1073741824L, 1073741824L, 0L))
> 
> should be accepted, right?
> 
> So, only the final `dtotal` needs to be compared with `R_XLEN_T_MAX`,
> outside the `for` loop. Function `allocArray()` should be like that, too.

excellent finding -- thank you, Suharto!
And indeed you are right:  whereas  allocArray() is not called too often from
R, it is in the API.

I've tried that and added more tests, finding that (old and new) R fail for an
extreme case which should work -- note: I am indeed aiming at case where the
product of dimensions overflows to `Inf` and then "would be" multiplied by 0
{which R's cumprod() does "correctly"}:
```
> array(integer(0), dim = c(rep(2^30, 35), 0))
Error in array(integer(0), dim = c(rep(2^30, 35), 0)) : 
  negative length vectors are not allowed
```
but the following works (after fix) and also in earlier R:
```
> a <- integer(0); dim(a) <- c(rep(2^30, 35), 0)
> str(a)
 int[1:1073741824, 1:1073741824, 1:1073741824, 1:1073741824, .......
     ....................
     1:1073741824, 0 ] 
> cumprod(dim(a))
 [1]  1.073742e+09  1.152922e+18  1.237940e+27  1.329228e+36  1.427248e+45 
1.532496e+54
................
[31] 9.076031e+279 9.745314e+288 1.046395e+298 1.123558e+307           Inf 
0.000000e+00
> 
```

I see a nice way to work via a  `dim2total()` auxiliary function  to be used at
least in 3 different cases, and which would ensure that also the above extreme
`array()` example works.

I'm re-opening the PR for now.

Tangentially related: when playing around with this behavior a bit, I also
noticed the following confusing error:


```
Sys.setlocale("LC_TIME", "zh_CN")
Sys.getlocale()
# [1]
"LC_CTYPE=en_US.UTF-8;LC_NUMERIC=C;LC_TIME=zh_CN;LC_COLLATE=en_US.UTF-8;LC_MONETARY=en_US.UTF-8;LC_MESSAGES=en_US.UTF-8;LC_PAPER=en_US.UTF-8;LC_NAME=C;LC_ADDRESS=C;LC_TELEPHONE=C;LC_MEASUREMENT=en_US.UTF-8;LC_IDENTIFICATION=C"

%b')

#   input string is too long

# c.f.
strftime(as.Date("2000-11-01"), "%Y %d %b")
# [1] "2000 01 11\xd4\xc2"
```

It's unusual to have this particular locale setting; more typical would be:

```
Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "zh_CN")
roundtrip()
# [1] "2000-11-01 UTC"
```

And this works too:

```
Sys.setlocale("LC_TIME", "zh_CN.utf8")
roundtrip()
# [1] "2000-11-01 UTC"
```

So it's because of a mismatch in the inferred encoding under `zh_CN` (GB2312).

*[Bug 19121] New: re-entrant calls to parse_Rd can crash R*
<https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=19121>

            Bug ID: 19121
           Summary: re-entrant calls to parse_Rd can crash R
           Product: R
           Version: R-devel (trunk)
          Hardware: Other
                OS: Other
            Status: NEW
          Severity: normal
          Priority: P5
         Component: Low-level
          Assignee: <mailto:R-core@R-project.org|R-core@R-project.org>
          Reporter: <mailto:kevinushey@gmail.com|kevinushey@gmail.com>

Created attachment 3770
  --> <https://bugs.r-project.org/attachment.cgi?id=3770&action=edit>
Candidate patch.

To reproduce:

```
tailn <- function(n) paste(sprintf("\\section{S%d}{body %d \\code{x%d}}",
                                   1:n, 1:n, 1:n), collapse = "\n")
outer <- tempfile(fileext=".Rd")
writeLines(paste0("\\name{o}\\title{T}\\description{d}\\eqn{a\nb}\n",
                  tailn(12), "\n"), outer)
inner <- tempfile(fileext=".Rd")
writeLines("\\name{i}\\title{IT}\\description{inner \\code{z}}\n", inner)

withCallingHandlers(
    tools::parse_Rd(outer),
    warning = function(w) {
        tools::parse_Rd(inner)          # <- re-entry
        invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    })
```

Such code is somewhat convoluted, but there is code in R itself that gets
"close" to this -- `tools:::processRdChunk` (`RdConv2.R:312-318`) calls
`parse_Rd` in a try block *and* in both its `warning` and `error` handlers, for
`\Sexpr[results=rd]` -- exactly the shape one would worry about, but happens to
be fine because `tryCatch` unwinds.

Exploring this identified a similar issue; the `busy` flag in the parser can
also get leaked if a longjmp occurs during the parse. The `mset` value is also
never copied or set in `PutState` / `UseState`.

The simplest fix here is to just catch and disallow re-entrant parsing of Rd
files in R, and also copy the `mset` field as appropriate.

%OS returns NA when encountering seconds outside [0,61)

`%OS` does not require its value to have `0 <= x < 61` as `%S` ostensibly does:

```
strptime("2023-01-01 12:00:99", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
# [1] NA
strptime("2023-01-01 12:00:99.0", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%OS")
# [1] "2023-01-01 12:00:00 UTC"
```

I don't see anything in `?strptime` suggesting this is intended behavior, so
I'm attaching a patch whereby it becomes `NA` in parity to the `%S` case.
